metas.text: Backtesting means simulating a trading strategy on historical data to estimate how it would have performed. Done well, it filters out bad ideas before they touch real capital. Done poorly, it manufactures false confidence. The most dangerous pitfall is look-ahead bias: accidentally using information that was not available at the time of the simulated trade. A classic example is ranking stocks on financial ratios from annual reports before those reports were actually published. The fix is

from annual reports before those reports were actually published. The fix is point-in-time data, where every input is timestamped by when it became known. Survivorship bias is the second trap. If your historical universe only contains companies that exist today, you have silently deleted every bankruptcy and delisting, which flatters the results. A proper backtest reconstructs the investable universe as it looked on each historical date. Overfitting is the third. With enough parameters, any

on each historical date. Overfitting is the third. With enough parameters, any strategy can be tuned to look brilliant in-sample. Defenses include keeping models simple, testing on out-of-sample periods, and demanding that performance hold across different market regimes and countries. Finally, a backtest is not reality: it usually ignores transaction costs, market impact, and the fact that publishing a strategy can erode its edge. Treat backtest returns as an upper bound, not a promise.

Credit risk modeling breaks expected loss into three components, together known as PD, LGD, and EAD. Expected loss equals PD times LGD times EAD. PD is the probability of default: the likelihood that a borrower fails to repay within a given horizon, usually one year. Banks estimate PD with statistical models, most commonly logistic regression on borrower characteristics such as credit score, income, debt-to-income ratio, and payment history. The model outputs a score that is calibrated into a

ratio, and payment history. The model outputs a score that is calibrated into a probability. LGD is loss given default: the share of the exposure the lender actually loses if default happens. A mortgage has low LGD because the house can be sold to recover most of the loan; an unsecured credit card has high LGD. EAD is exposure at default: the amount outstanding when default occurs, which for revolving credit includes an estimate of how much of the unused line the borrower will draw down first.

an estimate of how much of the unused line the borrower will draw down first. Regulators care deeply about these models. Under the Basel framework, banks using the internal ratings-based approach must estimate PD, LGD, and EAD themselves and hold capital against the results. Supervisors validate the models under guidance like SR 11-7, which demands conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring, and independent validation.

Dollar-cost averaging means investing a fixed amount of money on a regular schedule, regardless of market prices. For example, buying five hundred dollars of an index fund every month. When prices are high, the fixed sum buys fewer shares; when prices fall, it buys more. Over time the average cost per share sits below the average market price. The main appeal is behavioral, not mathematical. Most investors cannot time the market, and lump-sum investing at a peak is painful. A fixed schedule

time the market, and lump-sum investing at a peak is painful. A fixed schedule removes the decision entirely, which keeps people invested through downturns instead of panic-selling. Studies comparing lump-sum investing to dollar-cost averaging generally find that investing everything at once wins on average, because markets rise more often than they fall. Dollar-cost averaging wins on regret: it limits the damage of spectacularly bad timing and helps nervous investors participate at all. It

of spectacularly bad timing and helps nervous investors participate at all. It works best with low-cost diversified funds held for years. Applied to a single volatile stock, the same schedule concentrates risk rather than diversifying it. The schedule matters less than the habit: regular contributions, reinvested dividends, and the patience to leave the money alone.

Factor investing is the idea that stock returns can be explained by exposure to a small set of common characteristics, called factors. Instead of picking individual stocks based on stories, a factor investor systematically tilts a portfolio toward stocks with desirable traits. The best-known factors come from academic research. The value factor favors stocks that look cheap relative to fundamentals, for example a low price-to-earnings or price-to-book ratio. The momentum factor favors stocks

low price-to-earnings or price-to-book ratio. The momentum factor favors stocks whose prices have been rising over the past 6 to 12 months, on the evidence that trends persist. The quality factor favors profitable companies with stable earnings and low debt. The size factor favors smaller companies, which have historically earned a premium over large caps. The low-volatility factor favors stocks with calmer price movements. In practice, factor research follows a repeatable loop. First, define

In practice, factor research follows a repeatable loop. First, define the factor precisely, for example "book-to-market ratio in the top quintile." Second, build the signal for every stock in the universe at each point in time. Third, form portfolios that go long the favored stocks and short the opposite end, or simply overweight the favored names. Fourth, backtest the strategy on historical data and check whether the returns survive transaction costs. A critical discipline is distinguishing

the returns survive transaction costs. A critical discipline is distinguishing real factors from data mining. With thousands of candidate signals, some will look profitable by pure chance. Researchers therefore demand out-of-sample validation, economic intuition for why the factor should work, and persistence across countries and time periods before trusting a new factor.

The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, is the most quoted valuation multiple in equity markets. It is computed as the share price divided by earnings per share. A P/E of 20 means investors pay twenty dollars for each dollar of annual earnings. There are two main flavors. Trailing P/E uses the earnings of the past twelve months, which are known with certainty. Forward P/E uses analysts' estimates of next year's earnings, which reflect expectations but can be wrong. Growth stocks typically trade at

which reflect expectations but can be wrong. Growth stocks typically trade at high P/E ratios because investors expect earnings to expand; value stocks trade at low multiples. The ratio has well-known limits. Earnings can be depressed temporarily, making a healthy company look expensive. Companies with negative earnings have no meaningful P/E at all. Accounting choices also distort earnings, which is why some investors prefer multiples based on cash flow or sales. A common use is relative

prefer multiples based on cash flow or sales. A common use is relative comparison: a stock's P/E versus its own history, versus peers, or versus the market. A below-peer P/E may signal a bargain, or it may signal that the market correctly expects slower growth. The multiple alone never tells you which.

A 10-K is the annual report that US public companies must file with the Securities and Exchange Commission. It is the most comprehensive regular disclosure a company makes, and it is far more detailed than the glossy annual report sent to shareholders. The filing is organized into four parts. Part I describes the business itself: what the company sells, its markets, and risk factors. The risk factors section is worth reading carefully, because companies must disclose the things that could

worth reading carefully, because companies must disclose the things that could actually hurt them, from customer concentration to regulatory exposure. Part I also covers unresolved staff comments and cybersecurity disclosures. Part II contains the financial statements: the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement, plus management's discussion and analysis, known as MD&A. In MD&A, management explains in plain language why revenue, margins, and cash flow moved the way they did. It

plain language why revenue, margins, and cash flow moved the way they did. It is one of the best places to understand the business narrative behind the numbers. Part III covers governance: executive compensation, board members, and related-party transactions. Part IV lists exhibits, including the full financial statement schedules. The 10-K is filed on SEC EDGAR, where every filing is freely available as structured data, which makes it a favorite source for quantitative researchers building
